$comment: What pkinative can do, the export that does it, and the version that brought it — the machine-readable twin of docs/guides/choose.md. Satellites (pkinative-cli, pkinative-mcp) come after 1.0.0, as separate packages pinning pkinative ^1.0.0 (ROADMAP.md §1.0.0); until then every capability is library-only.

capabilities.capability: Fail with a typed error carrying a stable, machine-readable code, never a bare TypeError
Bound every loop over untrusted bytes with a named, CWE-tagged limit
Decode DER strictly, or BER on request, into a tree of zero-copy nodes
Read BOOLEAN, INTEGER, ENUMERATED, NULL, BIT STRING, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER, RELATIVE-OID, eight string types and both time types
Encode DER, refusing what DER cannot represent; re-encode a decoded tree byte for byte
Encode, decode and validate OIDs; name them from a registry of 300+ entries
Decode RFC 7468 PEM in strict or lax mode, optionally restricted to one label; encode PEM

Certificate fingerprints over SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, synchronous or through Web Crypto, the RFC 5280 key identifier that lets one certificate name the key of another, and SHAKE256 at any output length — the digest of an Ed448 CMS signer (RFC 8419 §3.1)
Parse an RFC 5280 certificate: every field, every standard extension, profile concerns as diagnostics
Verify a certificate signature against its issuer through Web Crypto — RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 and PSS, ECDSA on P-256/384/521, Ed25519 and Ed448
Build and sign an RFC 5280 certificate or a PKCS#10 request from a typed description, through a Web Crypto key the caller holds

Read a PKCS#10 certification request — subject, key, attributes and the extensions it asks for, held to the same readers, codes and bounds as a certificate — and verify its proof of possession with the key it carries; nothing here says a CA should grant it

Verify a certificate the whole way in one call — each signature verified the moment the path search is about to rely on it and never twice, then the host name, the purpose and revocation — because every layer below answers one question and somebody has to put them in the right order
Build and validate a certification path against a trust anchor (RFC 5280 §6) — synchronous, never throwing, backtracking past cross-signed issuers, and reporting every reason rather than the first

Check that a certificate names the host or address you connected to (RFC 6125) — a separate question from path validation, which has no notion of the name you asked for, and the one whose absence turns a valid certificate for somebody else into an accepted one
Ask whether a validated chain may be used for the purpose you need (RFC 5280 extKeyUsage) — a question section 6 never asks, and one where a CA own purpose restricts what it may issue for
Read an RFC 5280 CRL, verify its signature and decide a certificate's revocation status — the list is walked with a lazy cursor, never decoded into nodes, so a list of millions costs constant memory
Build an RFC 6960 OCSP request, read a response and verify its signature — good, revoked and unknown stay three states, because unknown is the responder saying it does not know

Read, create and verify an RFC 5652 CMS SignedData — a .p7s, an S/MIME signature, a PDF /Contents — signed through Web Crypto or an external signer such as an HSM, and verified in one call that keeps intact (unaltered) apart from valid (unaltered and trusted)

Request, read, verify and attach an RFC 3161 timestamp, and judge a signer at the time it proves — while the timestamp authority itself is judged at the time of verification, so a token cannot vouch for its own backdating

Read a PKCS#8 private key, plain or under PBES2, and describe it without exposing its secret — then turn it into a non-extractable Web Crypto signing key, an encrypted one unwrapped by the host so that its plaintext never becomes a JavaScript value; every other password scheme is named and refused with the conversion to run

Open a PKCS#12 (.p12, .pfx) in one call — an RFC 9579 PBMAC1 checked, every SafeContents opened, every certificate parsed, every key unwrapped as the algorithm of its certificate — with integrity that fails closed on the RFC 7292 Appendix B MAC nothing here computes; or read it without a password and open it one step at a time
